name: Cheek lift
lead: A cheek lift, also called a midface lift, is a cosmetic surgical procedure that repositions sagging soft tissue of the cheek, including the malar fat pad, to a higher position on the face. People use it to restore fullness over the cheekbones, soften the fold between nose and mouth and shorten the distance between the lower eyelid and the cheek, which is why it is usually discussed as a way to look fresher and more youthful [1][2][10]. It is performed under the broader heading of facial rejuvenation and is often combined with eyelid surgery or a full facelift [1][2].

Surgical descriptions in the literature include approaches through the lower eyelid, through the mouth and hairline, and by endoscope, with some techniques working beneath the periosteum, the membrane covering the facial bones [3][4][5][19][20]. Non-surgical alternatives marketed for lifting the cheeks, such as threads, fillers and energy-based devices, are discussed separately from surgical cheek lifts [6][7].

In looksmaxxing communities the procedure is discussed mainly by younger men who report a hollow, flat or aged look in the midface and ask how much a cheek lift would improve their appearance, often alongside under-eye fat grafting, cheek and jaw implants and rhinoplasty [18][21]. Published evidence on the procedure is largely surgeon-authored technique descriptions and case series, with a small number of controlled studies such as a randomised trial of midface lift combined with lipofilling [22].

paras: General references describe the midface lift as aimed at people whose main concern is flattening of the cheeks and deepening of the fold between nose and mouth, without marked jowling or neck laxity. Small incisions at the hairline and inside the mouth are used so that the fat pads over the cheekbones can be moved upward, which typically leaves few visible scars [1]. Wikipedia describes the procedure as commonly performed in patients in their forties, with a rather short recovery compared with a traditional facelift [1].

A 2015 review defines the midface as including both the lower lid subunit and the cheek down to the nasolabial fold, and lists the techniques used: skin tightening with direct excision, skin-muscle flaps, isolated fat pad transposition and subperiosteal lifting, with endoscopic subperiosteal midface lifting and endoscopic malar fat pad lifting discussed in detail [19]. A companion review describes how midface surgery evolved from laterally based rhytidectomy techniques with superolateral lifting to approaches with more vertical vectors, based on lower blepharoplasty techniques [20].

Surgeons have published several named variations. A 1999 report described a simplified subperiosteal cheek lift performed through the lower eyelid, developed as a modification of earlier endoscopic and eyelid-approach methods because the earlier eyelid approach required a lateral canthoplasty that added technical difficulty and risk of complications [2]. A 1998 paper described a subperiosteal approach to the midface termed the tridimensional functional cheek lift [4]. A 2017 report in Archives of Plastic Surgery described a technique titled facial rejuvenation enhancing cheek lift [5][3]. A 2023 review of advanced endoscopic techniques for Asian facial rejuvenation describes a 'Ponytail Lift' that simulates a vertical lift of the face through hidden incisions, reflecting the view that traditional SMAS facelifts were developed on white patients [24].

Other published options include midface lifts using an absorbable soft-tissue suspension device, examined in a 2006 clinical trial [25], and endoscopic-assisted facelifting reviewed in 2014 and facelift techniques surveyed in a 2022 overview [26][27].

Wikipedia traces the facelift to 1901, when Eugen Hollander reportedly removed a strip of skin around the ears in Berlin at a patient's request to lift her cheeks and mouth corners. Charles Miller published a textbook in 1907, Tord Skoog introduced subfascial dissection around 1968-1974, Mitz and Peyronie described the SMAS in 1976, and Paul Tessier's work on subperiosteal undermining of the orbital rims in the late 1970s and 1980s led to the deep-plane era and then to volumetric approaches from 1991 that lifted more vertically [1].

The article lists the mid face-lift among facelift variants alongside the SMAS, deep-plane, composite, mini, subperiosteal, skin-only and MACS lifts, and reports that facelifts were the third most popular aesthetic surgery in 2019 according to the American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery, after rhinoplasty and blepharoplasty [1]. It also says male patients present specific challenges, such as hair-bearing preauricular skin and the risk of sideburns being pulled upward and backward [1].

Cheek volume can also be addressed without repositioning tissue. A 2005 review of facial sculpting discussed dermal and subdermal fillers used to support the brow, the tear-trough area and the malar region, as part of an expansion of fillers into roles formerly handled by surgery [6]. Thread lifts, which use suture threads to suspend tissue, are described as a minimally invasive option, though a general reference notes concern over variable training of practitioners [7][8].

Lower eyelid and cheek surgery are often linked. A 2005 review describes transconjunctival fat repositioning, moving herniated lower-lid fat into the nasojugal fold to avoid a hollow lid, and notes it can be combined with an endoscopic subperiosteal midface lift [23]. A 2021 randomised controlled trial studied primary subperiosteal midface lift with simultaneous lipofilling in patients with negative lower eyelid vectors, on the premise that fat grafting is a necessary adjunct in that group [22]. For eyelids retracted after blepharoplasty, a 2021 review describes a hand-carved ePTFE implant on the orbital rim to provide volume and anchor lifted cheek tissue [28].
In Asian patients with prominent cheekbones, a 2016 report described combining reduction malarplasty with a facelift to counter cheek descent that can follow bone reduction in older patients [9].

Wikipedia lists haematoma as the most common facelift complication, usually within 24 hours, along with nerve injury (the greater auricular nerve is the most commonly injured sensory nerve and the facial nerve the most commonly injured motor nerve), hypertrophic scarring, permanent hair loss at temporal incisions, and skin necrosis, with smoking raising the risk roughly twelvefold; patients are typically asked to stop aspirin or blood thinners at least a week beforehand [1].

Midface-specific publications in the literature include reports on lower-eyelid malposition and retraction as a complication of eyelid and cheek surgery, treated with revision procedures, including spacer grafts [10][11][28][29]. A 2005 clinical trial examined the effect of endoscopic forehead and midface lifting on lower eyelid tension [30], and a 2005 study examined the effect of rhytidectomy on the nasal valve [12].

Published surgical literature on cheek lifts consists mostly of technique descriptions and case series by the surgeons who developed the methods [2][4][5]. Controlled work exists in a few places, including the 2021 randomised trial of midface lift with lipofilling [22], a 2005 clinical trial of lower-eyelid tension after endoscopic lifting [30] and a 2006 clinical trial of an absorbable suspension device [25].

Registered trials exist for non-surgical lifting products and devices in the midface. These include a completed 144-participant trial of hyaluronic-acid-coated and uncoated threads for midface lifting and nasolabial fold correction [13], a completed 103-participant study of an ultrasound system for lifting and tightening cheek tissue [14], a 45-participant trial of a laser-type device for lax skin [15], a 54-participant study of lifting and tightening in darker skin [31] and a 45-participant study combining threads with microfocused ultrasound [16]. Their results are not summarised in the registry records cited here.

A 2011 study quantified errors that arise when standardised facial photography is not followed, noting that photographs are used for documentation of before-and-after results in plastic surgery and that subtle changes are easy to misjudge in non-standard images [17].

On looksmax.org, cheek lifts come up as a hardmaxx option for men who feel their cheeks look flat or aged; discussion is small and mostly consists of users asking how much it would change their rating [18]. In one thread a poster calls it a 'dream surgery', possibly with under-eye fat grafting, that he feels he needs to look his age and compete with higher-rated men; a reply describes planning tanning and cardio to lower body fat and trying facial exercises [18]. Another thread shows a patient result with cheek, chin and jaw implants, rhinoplasty and a midface lift, with replies commenting on how leaner the patient could look and on hair [21].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, cheek lifts come up as a hardmaxx option for men who feel their cheeks look flat or aged; discussion is small and mostly consists of users asking how much it would change their rating [18][21].

claims.claim: A cheek lift would make a large difference to how old and attractive a young man looks.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster calls it a dream surgery that, possibly with under-eye fat grafting, he needs in order to look like his age-mates and to compete with higher-rated men [18].
claims.experts: Published sources describe the procedure chiefly for ageing faces with cheek descent, and report technique series rather than appearance-rating outcomes in young men [1][2].

claims.claim: Tanning, cardio and lower body fat can reduce the aged look of the malar area without surgery.
claims.believers: A reply in the same thread says he plans tanning and cardio to lower body-fat percentage, and that in harsh light he looks 60 years old [18].
claims.experts: No published studies address tanning or fat loss as a substitute for midface lifting.

claims.claim: Facial exercises quickly reduce the appearance of malar fat pads.
claims.believers: One user reports that after one week of facial exercises the appearance of malar fat pads was significantly reduced and says he planned to start a thread about it [18].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested facial exercises for malar fat pad appearance; surgical and filler literature addresses the area by repositioning or adding volume [2][6].

claims.claim: A cheek lift can be combined with implants, rhinoplasty and other surgery for a full facial result.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org member posts a combined cheek, chin and jaw implant, rhinoplasty and midface lift result and says he is highly satisfied seven months on; replies comment on leanness and hair [21].
claims.experts: Surgical references describe the midface lift as often combined with eyelid surgery or a facelift [1], and a trial design pairs lift with fat grafting in negative-vector patients [22]; no study of multi-procedure looksmaxxing-style combinations was found.

claims.claim: Fat grafting is needed alongside a lift when the eye projects beyond the cheek.
claims.believers: Forum posters discuss pairing a cheek lift with under-eye fat grafting [18].
claims.experts: A 2021 randomised controlled trial studied midface lift plus lipofilling in patients with negative lower eyelid vectors, working from the premise that lipofilling is a necessary adjunct [22]; the abstract summarised here does not give outcome figures.

card.summary: Surgical repositioning of sagging cheek tissue, studied mainly in ageing faces; looksmaxxing talk about it for young men is largely untested.
card.note: Evidence is mostly surgeon-reported technique series; surgical risks include nerve injury, haematoma and eyelid complications.

quick.overview:
A cheek lift, or midface lift, moves sagging cheek tissue and fat upward. Most published descriptions come from surgeons treating ageing faces, often alongside eyelid surgery or a facelift.

On looksmax.org it is mentioned by men who think their cheeks look flat or hollow and wonder how much it would change their appearance. There is little published evidence on that use.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons lift the cheek soft tissue, sometimes beneath the periosteum, through incisions at the lower eyelid, hairline or inside the mouth, and fix it in a higher position. Non-surgical options such as threads, fillers and ultrasound devices are used for milder cases.
quick.risks: General facelift references list haematoma, nerve injury, scarring and eyelid malposition among possible complications; smoking raises the risk of skin necrosis. Surgical cheek-lift results are documented mainly in surgeon-authored series rather than controlled trials.

angle.goal: Midface fullness and a younger-looking cheek
chain: Surgeon releases and lifts the cheek soft tissue and malar fat pad
Tissue is fixed in a higher position over the cheekbone
Cheek looks fuller and higher, the lid-cheek line shorter and the nasolabial fold softer
angle.text: A cheek lift repositions sagging cheek tissue upward, which people use to counter flattening of the cheeks and deepening of the fold between nose and mouth. Some surgeons combine it with fat grafting, eyelid surgery or implants when the lower eyelid and cheek also need volume or support.
